5SI ENGLISH  ·  INFERRING CHARACTER
Unit 1 · Week 2 · Lesson 8
L8 The skill first. Two texts to apply it to.

Reading a
Character

How do we know what a character is really like? A writer almost never tells us straight out. We read the evidence they leave, infer the trait, then prove it in their own words. Today is about getting good at that one move.

✎
The move: a detail is evidence → the trait is your inference → the words are your proof.
1 Learning objective

To infer what a character is really like from a writer’s evidence, and prove each inference in the words of the text.

Success criteria

  • I can find where character is hidden: speech, thoughts, effect, actions, looks.
  • I can turn a detail into a precise trait, not just “nice” or “mean”.
  • I can explain how the exact words create that impression.
  • I can test what a character says against what they do.

Why it matters

Every reading question that asks “what is this character like?” is testing inference. Retelling the plot earns nothing. The marks live in evidence, trait and explanation.

By the end you will meet a poem and a fable, and do exactly this with both.

2 The big idea

Writers show. You infer.

Telling (rare, flat)

“He was greedy.”

→
Showing (what writers do)

“He reached for the last slice before the others had finished their first.”

Nobody wrote the word “greedy”. You supplied it. That leap, from a shown detail to a named trait, backed by the words, is the whole skill for today.

Starter · Quick fire

One detail. What kind of person?

“She apologised to the door she had walked into.”

Perhaps: flustered, self-effacing, polite by reflex.

“He alphabetised the spice rack on his first night in the new flat.”

Perhaps: orderly, precise, needs control.

“The new kid had given away half his lunch by the end of week one.”

Perhaps: generous, or anxious to belong.

“She read the last page of every book first.”

Perhaps: impatient, anxious, likes to be in control.

💡
A good inference is reasoned from the detail, not a wild guess. And one detail can point two ways.
Starter · Detective

A bag is left on the train. Who owns it?

Inside

a dog-eared novel · a half-eaten protein bar · three different pens, all chewed · a birthday card, still sealed in its envelope

What can we infer?

  • A reader, on the move, always a little rushed.
  • Restless or anxious (the chewed pens).
  • Forgetful, or a procrastinator (the unsent card).
💡
Every trait was earned from an object. That is exactly how writers work: the detail carries the meaning.
Starter · Both directions

Turn tell into show, and show into tell.

Prove the trait

“She was nervous.”

Give three shown details that would let a reader infer it. No feelings words allowed.

e.g. re-read the same line four times, bit the skin by her thumb, kept glancing at the door.

Name the trait

“He gave away his umbrella and walked home soaked.”

What single, precise word does this show?

e.g. selfless, generous, or a martyr who wants it noticed.

Starter · Mind the gap

When words and actions disagree, believe the actions.

“I’m not bothered,” he said, checking the results for the fourth time.

Real read: he is very bothered. The action exposes the words.

“Take the bigger piece,” she insisted, sliding it back to herself when he refused.

Real read: the generosity is a performance. Watch the hands, not the mouth.

⚠
Hold on to this one. It is the key that unlocks Fox later.
Lens · Where to look

Five places a writer hides character

S
Speech

What they say, and how they say it.

T
Thoughts

What they reveal on the inside.

E
Effect

How others react to them.

A
Actions

What they choose to do.

L
Looks

Appearance and body language.

🔍
Stuck on a text? Run S·T·E·A·L and ask each one: what does this show?
Lens · How it is told

The writer chose that word on purpose.

Neutral

“a loud sound”

Loaded

“a cruel clang”

Inference

the bell is an enemy, not just noisy

Same event, different word, different character. “Cruel” carries intent and menace. When you annotate, hunt the loaded word and ask what it makes the reader feel about the character.

Template · The mark-earning chain

Evidence → Inference → Explanation

Evidence

“a cruel clang”

A short quotation you can point to.

→
Inference

The speaker treats the bell as a deliberate enemy.

→
Explanation

“cruel” adds intent, as if a lifeless object chooses to hurt.

The word “” suggests because .

Template · Say it precisely

Ban the flat word. Reach for the sharp one.

Instead of
Reach for
clever
cunning · shrewd · calculating · resourceful
trusting
credulous · naive · guileless
kind
magnanimous · considerate · selfless
selfish
callous · self-serving · ruthless
confident
self-possessed · assured · brazen
honest
candid · earnest · forthright
🎯
A precise trait already contains an argument. “Calculating” says more than “clever” in a single word.
Template · Upgrade the inference

From a guess to an argument.

Weak

“Fox is clever.”

Strong

“Fox is calculating and self-serving: she plans her own escape while Goat still drinks, then uses him as a ladder and abandons him.”

The anatomy of a strong inference: a precise trait, the evidence that proves it, and what it implies. All three, in one breath.

Template · The truth test

A character’s claim is not automatically true.

Says

“there’s plenty for us both”

Sounds generous, sharing, warm.

Does

climbs out on Goat’s back and leaves him trapped

Acts entirely for herself.

Real character = duplicitous. The gap between the words and the deeds is where the truth usually sits. Always cross-check a claim against an action.

I do · Modelled

Watch me run the whole move on one line.

“Greetings, Goat,” Fox cheerfully replied, disguising the sad facts of her predicament.”

Lens (STEAL)

Speech, plus the narrator’s aside about her.

Trait (precise)

Composed and calculating, not panicked.

Explain

“cheerfully” while trapped shows control; “disguising” tells us she is already scheming.

We do · Together on the board

Your turn to drive. Build the chain.

“Unable to think beyond his thirst, parched Goat replied…”

Model: Goat is impulsive: “unable to think beyond” shows his need blocks all judgement, which is why he leaps without a plan.

“Yet by my bedside you must dwell.”

Model: the speaker feels trapped: “must” removes all choice, so hatred and dependence sit side by side.

✍
Push for the precise trait first, then make them prove it in the exact words.
You do · Pairs

Trait detective. Name it, then prove it.

“He counted the change twice, then slid the extra coin into his own pocket.”

e.g. dishonest, opportunistic.

“She stayed behind to stack the chairs nobody had asked her to stack.”

e.g. conscientious, considerate.

“He laughed loudest at his own joke, glancing round to see who had noticed.”

e.g. insecure, vain.

💬
Task: for each, agree one precise trait, then write a single sentence proving it from the quotation.
You do · Stretch

A character is rarely just one thing.

Place Goat on the line. Where does the evidence put him, and could you argue for two spots?

naive
shrewd
leaps in blindly

Now pick a character you know well. Name two traits that pull against each other, with a piece of evidence for each. Complex beats simple every time.

3 Now apply it · Text 1
I do not like you, wake-up bell!
The reasons why I cannot tell -
And yet I know, and know full well -
I do not like you, wake-up bell.
Your cruel clang shatters slumber’s spell!
The sting of this I cannot quell.
Yet deep I know, know all too well -
I do not like you, wake-up bell.
Sleep, embrace me in your spell,
Your tender hush! My heart can tell
We’ll soon be parted with a yell -
From slumber’s rival - wake-up bell.
I’ll never like you, wake-up bell,
Demolishing sleep’s restful spell.
Yet by my bedside you must dwell.
I do not like you, wake-up bell.

Two characters: the speaker, and a personified bell. Run the lenses on both.

3 Now apply it · Text 2

Fox and Goat · track both characters.

The situation

Fox falls into a well. A thirsty Goat looks in. Fox hides her predicament, tempts Goat down, uses him to climb out and leaves him stuck.

Full text is on the worksheet, coming up next.

Bring your tools

STEAL to find the evidence. The says vs does test on Fox. The word bank to name traits precisely. The chain to prove them.

Aim for three traits each, with evidence. Do not retell the plot.

4 Worksheets

You’ve got the skill.
Now apply it.

Annotate on the sheets, answer the questions in your notebook. Everything you need, you have just practised.

Before you write: precise quotation → precise trait → explanation. If a sentence only retells what happens, cut it.

5 Exit ticket

Any character you have ever met.

Name one precise trait, and prove it in a single sentence of evidence.

No flat words. No plot retelling. Just evidence → trait → explanation, the move you own now.
